ta-l1d19q1-d1e3498.summary: A divisio textus opening Lombard's treatment of the equality of the divine persons (Distinctions 19–21), after their distinction by eternal relations. He shows their equality and then (Dist. 21) treats a doubt arising from expressions used in the proof. He first shows in what equality consists: eternity, magnitude, and power, which are really the same as the divine essence. Then he shows equality in each: eternity (already shown), magnitude, and power (Dist. 20). Equality in magnitude is proved three ways: from mutual indwelling (the Father is in the Son, the Son in the Father, and the Spirit in both); from the removal of what could cause inequality; and from divine simplicity and truth. It is concluded that God is called triune but not triple. Two inquiries are announced, on equality itself and on what it consists in. The first has two articles: whether there is equality in God, and whether it is mutual.
claims: The persons are equal in eternity, magnitude, and power, which are really the divine essence.
Mutual indwelling of the persons is a sign of their equality.
God is triune, not triple.

ta-l1d19q1-d1e3544.summary: First argument against equality in God. One in quantity makes equal (the Philosopher), and there is no quantity in God, who is great without quantity (Augustine).
claims: Equality requires quantity, which God lacks.

ta-l1d19q1-d1e3547.summary: Second argument. Whatever is absolute in God signifies the divine substance, and unity of substance grounds identity, not equality. So proving one essence of three persons proves identity rather than equality.
claims: Unity of substance makes identity, not equality.

ta-l1d19q1-d1e3550.summary: Third argument. Quality fits spiritual things better than quantity, since some species of quality (knowledge, virtue) are in spiritual substances but no species of quantity except perhaps number, which is not the basis of this equality. Since quality grounds likeness rather than equality, agreement in essential attributes should be called likeness rather than equality.
claims: Quality grounds likeness, and spiritual things have quality rather than quantity.

ta-l1d19q1-d1e3554.summary: Fourth argument. Every equality implies proportion and commensuration, and there is no commensuration of infinites. The divine persons are infinite, so there is no equality among them.
claims: Infinites admit no proportion.

ta-l1d19q1-d1e3557.summary: Sed contra from the Athanasian Creed: the three persons are coeternal and coequal.
claims: The three persons are coequal.

ta-l1d19q1-d1e3563.summary: Thomas's determination. One in substance makes the same, one in quantity equal, one in quality like (the Philosopher). Although quality and quantity in their common generic character are not in God, some species of quality are there by their constitutive differences, and some species of quantity, such as magnitude and duration, by what is proper to them. So equality and likeness are said in God. As what is signified as quality, like wisdom, differs from the essence only conceptually, so likeness and identity in God differ conceptually, not really, and the same holds of equality. So equality and likeness are found differently in God and in other things. In other equal things the quantity is not the same in essence but only by commensuration, and the quality is one only in species, since in them quality and essence differ, and essence regards being as its proper act. Quality and quantity are not said with respect to being but signify only the quiddity of a genus, so there can be one quantity where there is not one being, but there can be one essence absolutely only where there is one being, which is where the essence is numerically the same. So numerical unity is not required for equality but is required for identity. In the divine persons magnitude and wisdom are the same as the essence, so their equality and likeness consist in numerically the same wisdom and magnitude.
claims: Equality and likeness are in God through species of quantity and quality taken by their differences, not their genus.
In God equality, likeness, and identity differ only conceptually.
Equality in creatures requires only unity of species; in God it consists in numerically the same magnitude.

ta-l1d19q1-d1e3566.summary: Reply to the first argument. Equality is caused not only by unity in quantity by its common concept but also by the concept of a species of quantity, since unity of number or of time suffices for equality, and so there can be equality in God properly. Better: what is found in many belongs to them by what is common, so equality follows the common concept of quantity, which consists in divisibility. Quantity is found properly in what is divided in itself, which does not fit God, and in a way in what is divided by what is external to it, as virtue is called divisible and quantified by the concept and division of acts and objects. Such virtual quantity fits God, and therefore equality.
claims: Equality in God follows virtual quantity, measured by acts and objects.

ta-l1d19q1-d1e3569.summary: Reply to the second argument. As shown in Distinction 9, identity implies numerical unity of essence, and since in creatures, from which we take names said of God, unity of essence is found only in the same supposit, identity implies no distinction of supposit but rather unity. So the Son cannot be called 'the same' (idem, masculine) as the Father, only 'the same thing' (idem, neuter), with the unity referred to the essence. Equality and likeness imply unity of quantity or quality not by essence or being, and by their meaning do not imply numerical unity, only sameness in species, which exists in different supposits. So equality and likeness imply distinction together with unity, and we call the Son like or equal to the Father but not the same. That is why Lombard treated equality rather than identity: identity implies only unity of essence and does not fit the persons in every mode (not masculine), while equality implies both unity of essence, signified as quantity, and distinction of persons.
claims: Equality and likeness imply both unity and distinction, so they fit the persons; identity implies only unity.
The Son is 'idem' with the Father only in the neuter.

ta-l1d19q1-d1e3572.summary: Reply to the third argument. Although likeness also implies both unity and distinction (Hilary: likeness is not to oneself), equality adds something to likeness and includes it when said of the divine persons. Since in God there is only quantity of power, which is founded on quality, unity of such quantity posits unity of quality and excludes any excess of intensity: whatever are equal in colour are also alike, but not conversely.
claims: Equality includes likeness and adds the exclusion of any excess.

ta-l1d19q1-d1e3576.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Equality is a species of proportion, a proportion of things having one quantity. It is predicated of God by its differentia, having one quantity, not by its genus, commensuration of quantity. Divine magnitude is in no way measurable or measured, by another or by itself. First, measurement implies limitation, and divine magnitude has no limit within or without, so it is called infinite not privatively by extension but by negation of limit. Second, commensuration is of two quantities, not of one with itself, and no other magnitude can equal God's; Father and Son do not have different magnitudes but one and the same, by which they are equal, so nothing distinct is commensurate with divine magnitude. Third, as all motion reduces to a mover unmoved by itself or another, all measurement reduces to one first that is in no way measured but is the measure of all, God, as the Commentator says.
claims: Equality is said of God by its differentia (one quantity), not its genus (commensuration).
Divine magnitude is unmeasured, infinite by negation, and the measure of all.

ta-l1d19q1-d1e3588.summary: First argument against mutual equality. Dionysius says we do not admit conversion of likeness and equality between cause and caused. In God there is principle and what is from a principle, so the Son, from the Father as principle, is like and equal to the Father but not conversely.
claims: Likeness between cause and effect is not mutual.

ta-l1d19q1-d1e3591.summary: Second argument. Each thing is equal to what it is not less than, and nothing is equal to what it is greater than. Hilary says the Son is not less than the Father and yet the Father is greater than the Son, so the Son is equal to the Father but not conversely.
claims: Hilary: the Father is greater though the Son is not less.

ta-l1d19q1-d1e3597.summary: Third argument. Since nothing is equal to itself, whatever is called equal presupposes something it is equal to. The Son by order of nature presupposes the Father, while the Father presupposes nothing.
claims: Equality presupposes another.

ta-l1d19q1-d1e3601.summary: Sed contra from the Creed: the three persons are coeternal and coequal to one another, so there is mutual equality.
claims: The persons are coequal to one another.

ta-l1d19q1-d1e3607.summary: Thomas's determination. Since equality is founded on unity of quantity, to be equal to something is to have its quantity, and to be like it is to have its quality. A thing's quality is that which it has properly and fully. Sometimes the quality is perfectly in both and can be said to be of both, so each is like the other. Sometimes it is properly and fully in one, and in the other only as an imitation by participation, and then it is said to be the quality only of the one possessing it fully. Then what does not fully have it is called like what does, and not conversely: a picture is like a man, but properly speaking a man is not like his image. Moreover, 'to be assimilated' adds to 'to be like' a kind of motion and approach to unity of quality, and 'to be equalized' likewise to quantity. In the divine persons there is no motion, but in place of motion there is reception, as one person receives from another, so assimilation or equalization can be there only by reason of reception. Since magnitude or goodness is fully in each divine person, each can be called equal or like to the other. But since one person receives from another and not conversely, the receiving person can be said to be equalized or assimilated to the one from whom it receives, and not conversely. So there is mutual likeness and equality between Father and Son, but not mutual equalization or assimilation: the Son is equalized and assimilated to the Father, not conversely.
claims: Since each person fully possesses the divine magnitude, equality and likeness among them are mutual.
Equalization and assimilation, implying reception, are not mutual: the Son is equalized to the Father, not conversely.
concepts: likeness by participation vs. full possession

ta-l1d19q1-d1e3610.summary: Reply to the first argument. Dionysius speaks of caused things that do not perfectly receive their cause's likeness, which is not the case among the divine persons, since the Father's whole fullness is in the Son, so mutual likeness or equality can be said. Dionysius himself says that among coordinated, i.e. equal, things they can be like each other and convert likeness to each other.
claims: The Father's whole fullness is in the Son, so likeness is mutual.

ta-l1d19q1-d1e3613.summary: Reply to the second argument. 'The Father is greater than the Son' posits no degree of magnitude but only an order of authority, so it does not remove mutual equality, only mutual equalization.
claims: 'Greater' in Hilary signifies order of authority, not magnitude.

ta-l1d19q1-d1e3616.summary: Reply to the third argument. Equality does not necessarily presuppose something else but supposes it, so what is called equal need not have any order of priority or principle relative to what it is equal to, or conversely.
claims: Equality supposes another term but implies no order of priority.

ta-l1d19q1-Dd1e3493.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 19 opens Lombard's treatment of the equality of the persons in eternity, magnitude, and power, which are really the essence, with proofs of equal magnitude from mutual indwelling, removal of inequality, and simplicity. It announces inquiries into equality and its bases.
claims: The persons are equal in eternity, magnitude, and power.

ta-l1d19q1-Dd1e3536.summary: Article 1 asks whether there is equality in God. Thomas holds that equality and likeness are in God through species of quantity (magnitude, duration) and quality (wisdom), taken by their differentiae, not their genus. In God equality, likeness, and identity differ only conceptually, and the persons' equality consists in numerically the same magnitude. Equality follows virtual quantity. It fits the persons better than identity because it implies both unity and distinction, the Son being 'idem' only in the neuter. Equality includes likeness and adds exclusion of excess, and it is said of God by its differentia, one quantity, since divine magnitude is unmeasured and the measure of all.
claims: There is equality in God through numerically one magnitude.
Equality fits the persons because it implies unity with distinction.

ta-l1d19q1-Dd1e3580.summary: Article 2 asks whether equality in God is mutual. Thomas holds that because each person fully possesses the divine magnitude and goodness, equality and likeness are mutual. Equalization and assimilation, which imply reception in place of motion, are not mutual: the Son is equalized to the Father, not conversely. Hilary's 'greater' signifies only order of authority.
claims: Equality among the persons is mutual; equalization is not.

ta-l1d19q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 19 opens the treatment of the equality of the divine persons. Article 1 holds that equality and likeness exist in God through species of quantity and quality taken by their differentiae, so that the persons are equal by numerically one magnitude. In God equality, likeness, and identity differ only conceptually, and equality fits the persons better than identity because it signifies unity of essence together with distinction of persons. Divine magnitude is unmeasured and the measure of all. Article 2 holds that equality and likeness among the persons are mutual, since each possesses the divine magnitude fully, while equalization and assimilation, implying reception, belong only to the person who receives from another.
claims: The divine persons are equal by numerically one magnitude.
Equality is mutual among the persons, though only the receiving person is 'equalized' to the giver.
Equality signifies unity of essence together with distinction of persons.
